title: Matthew Was Probably Making Good Money—So Why Did He Walk Away?
paragraphs: Matthew Was Probably Making Good Money—So Why Did He Walk Away?

We cannot honestly calculate Matthew’s salary from Scripture. But what the Bible does tell us about his occupation makes the moment Jesus called him far more costly—and far more beautiful—than many readers realize.
There is a dangerous way to read Matthew 9:9.
We can read it too quickly.
Jesus walks by. Matthew is sitting there. Jesus says, “Follow Me.” Matthew gets up. End of story.
A few seconds on the page.
But imagine refusing to turn the page.
Stay at the booth.
Look at the money.
Look at the ledgers.
Look at the merchandise passing through.
Look at the man everyone knows.
Then listen to the footsteps of Jesus getting closer.
Because Matthew was not sitting beside a fishing net when Christ called him.
He was sitting at a place where money changed hands.
And that changes the emotional weight of everything.
The Greek text of Matthew 9:9 says:
Καὶ παράγων ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐκεῖθεν εἶδεν ἄνθρωπον καθήμενον ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον, Μαθθαῖον λεγόμενον... Ἀκολούθει μοι.
At the heart of the scene is one revealing word:
τελώνιον — telōnion.

It means a tax or toll booth, a place where customs were collected. The NET translators specifically note that we should not imagine a comfortable modern government office. Such booths could be situated where goods entered or passed through a town or port so customs duties and tolls could be collected.
Matthew was sitting where commerce met taxation.
Then Jesus arrived.
And before we ask how much Matthew made, we need to admit something Scripture never tells us.
The Bible gives us no salary figure for Matthew.
No annual income.
No commission percentage.
No surviving payslip.
No verse tells us Matthew earned the ancient equivalent of $50,000, $100,000, or any other modern amount.
So when someone confidently announces an exact salary for Matthew, they have moved beyond what the biblical text can establish.
We should not manufacture numbers to make Scripture dramatic.
Scripture is already dramatic enough.
What we can say is that Matthew was a τελώνης — telōnēs, a tax collector. Matthew 10:3 even preserves the designation beside his name: Matthew “the tax collector.”
That occupation mattered.
Matthew was not merely a man with a job.
He was a man associated with a profession that carried enormous social and moral baggage in the Gospel world.
And the story immediately shows us the company in which tax collectors were commonly placed.

After Matthew's call, Jesus eats with tax collectors and people publicly regarded as sinners. The Pharisees object to precisely that company, asking why Jesus eats with them. Christ responds with the language of sickness, mercy, and sinners needing His call.
Think about what that means emotionally.
Matthew may have known how to count money while wondering whether anybody still counted him worthy of love.
He could collect from other people while carrying something inside himself nobody could collect away.
He could sit at a booth surrounded by transactions and still have a bankrupt soul.
And maybe that is where this stops being an article about Matthew.
Maybe this is where it becomes an article about us.
Because you do not need to be a first-century tax collector to understand what it means to build a life that looks profitable from the outside and becomes expensive on the inside.
Some people make good money and cannot sleep.
Some have the career but lost the marriage.
Some built the reputation but buried the secret.
Some gained followers and lost themselves.
Some sit in church every Sunday while quietly wondering whether Jesus could possibly want the version of them nobody else knows exists.
Some have become so good at surviving that nobody realizes they are bleeding.
Matthew's booth had money in it.
But money could not say what Jesus was about to say.
Ἀκολούθει μοι — Akolouthei moi.
“Follow Me.”
The verb ἀκολούθει carries the sense of following, accompanying, going in the same way with someone. In Matthew 9:9 it appears as a command addressed directly to Matthew.
Not:
“Clean yourself up and perhaps I will reconsider you.”
Not:
“Pay back enough first and then approach Me.”
Not:
“Convince these religious people that you deserve another chance.”
Jesus saw him.
Jesus called him.
And Matthew got up.
καὶ ἀναστὰς ἠκολούθησεν αὐτῷ
He rose and followed Him.
Do not miss the violence hidden inside that quiet sentence.
Matthew stood up from the place where his old life worked.
Fishermen who followed Jesus could conceivably return to fishing. Boats still floated. Nets could be repaired.

But Matthew's occupation involved a position at a revenue point. The text does not tell us whether his particular post could ever have been reclaimed, so we should not romanticize details we cannot prove.
Yet the scene unquestionably presents a decisive movement.
He was sitting.
Christ called.
Matthew rose.
He followed.
Whatever Matthew's precise income had been, the point of the Gospel is not that Jesus offered him a better compensation package.
Jesus offered him Jesus.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
We live in a world obsessed with asking, “How much does it pay?”
Matthew's story forces another question:
What is it costing your soul?
What if the thing paying you is possessing you?
What if the relationship you refuse to surrender is slowly teaching you to live without obedience?
What if the applause has become your master?
What if your hidden sin gives you five minutes of pleasure and steals another piece of your peace every night?
What if you have spent years building the booth Jesus is asking you to leave?
That is where Christianity becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not come merely to become an accessory to the life we already designed.
He is Lord.
Grace is free, but following Christ rearranges allegiances.
Jesus later asks the terrifying question: what does it profit someone to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?
Matthew's booth makes that question visible.
Coins on one side.
Christ on the other.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is that Jesus knew exactly who was sitting there.
Matthew did not surprise Him.
His profession did not surprise Him.
His reputation did not surprise Him.
His past did not make Jesus hesitate.
εἶδεν ἄνθρωπον
He saw a man.
Before the crowd saw a category, Jesus saw a person.
Before people could reduce him to “tax collector,” Christ saw the human being sitting behind the title.
And somebody reading this desperately needs that truth.
Jesus sees you behind what happened.
Behind what you did.
Behind what was done to you.
Behind the addiction you keep renaming.
Behind the browser history.
Behind the private messages.
Behind the bitterness.
Behind the religious performance.
Behind the smile you put on before entering church.
Behind the sentence, “I'm fine.”
He sees.
But biblical grace never means Jesus looks at our sin and says it does not matter.
Grace means the sinner can be called out of the old life because mercy has come near.
This becomes unmistakable in what happens next.
Jesus is at the table with tax collectors and sinners, and religious observers are offended.
Then Christ says that healthy people do not need a physician, but sick people do. He tells His hearers to learn the meaning of, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,” and says He came to call sinners.
The Physician does not deny the disease.
He comes for the diseased.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin is harmless.
He saves sinners.
He forgives sinners.
He transforms sinners.
Ultimately He goes to the cross for sinners, bears sin, dies, and rises again victorious.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Your old life was fine.”
It is Christ saying, in effect:
Leave the booth. Follow Me.
And suddenly Matthew's income is not the most interesting thing about Matthew anymore.
That may be the answer you did not expect when you clicked this article.
How much did Matthew make?
We do not know.
Perhaps his work gave him a financially advantageous life compared with many around him; the text simply does not give us enough information to calculate it responsibly.
But we know something infinitely more important.
When Jesus called, Matthew discovered Someone worth more than whatever was sitting on that table.
That is the wealth of the story.
Not Matthew's coins.
Matthew's Christ.
And then grace does something beautiful.
The man at the tax booth becomes part of the apostolic company. Matthew 10:2–4 names Matthew among the Twelve and uniquely remembers him there as “the tax collector.”
Think about that.
His past was not erased from the vocabulary.
It was reinterpreted by grace.
“The tax collector” became a disciple of Jesus.
A scandalous history became part of a testimony.
That does not mean the past became good.
It means the past no longer got the final word.
This is what Jesus does.
He does not merely improve résumés.
He resurrects lives.
He takes people with histories.
People with regrets.
People who chose money over integrity.
People who compromised.
People who lied.
People who wasted years.
People who feel spiritually disqualified.
People everybody else has already categorized.
And He calls sinners to Himself.
Repentance means we do not remain comfortably seated at the booth while claiming to follow Jesus.
There comes a moment when grace demands a response.
Matthew rose.
Maybe your “booth” is not money.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe pride.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe greed.
Maybe the need to impress everyone.
Maybe secret dishonesty.
Maybe a relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
Maybe religious hypocrisy.
Maybe you have become extremely successful at looking Christian without actually surrendering to Christ.
You know the booth.
And worse...
you may already know what Jesus has been telling you about it.
There is something terrifying about staying seated when Christ says, “Follow Me.”
But there is something unimaginably beautiful about standing up.
You may lose something.
Matthew's story never promises otherwise.
Following Jesus has always been more serious than adding inspirational Bible verses to an unchanged life.
But whatever obedience costs, Christ is greater.
Your sin cannot offer what His blood offers.
Your money cannot purchase what His grace gives.
Your reputation cannot provide what His forgiveness provides.
Your secret addiction cannot love you.
Your success cannot resurrect you.
Your possessions cannot die for you.
Jesus did.
And Jesus rose.
So perhaps the question was never merely:
“What was Matthew's income like?”
Perhaps the question hiding underneath it was:
“What could make a man get up from a profitable table and follow Jesus?”
The answer is not poverty.
The answer is not adventure.
The answer is not self-improvement.
The answer is a Person.
Jesus Christ.
If this exposed a booth in your own heart that you have been afraid to leave, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest before God.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Somebody reading underneath this article may need to discover that Jesus still transforms real people with real histories.
And do not keep this story trapped on your screen.
Not as a transaction with God. Not because clicking “share” earns divine favor. We are saved by God's grace through faith, and genuine good works flow from that grace.
But if this ministry is helping proclaim Christ, supporting and sharing it can be one practical way of participating in that work.

If you want your online presence to glorify God, let it carry something greater than entertainment. Share truth. Share Scripture. Share the Gospel. Send this article to the person whose “successful” life may secretly be crushing them.
One day the booth may start looking attractive again.
One day obedience may feel expensive.
Come back and remember Matthew standing up.
Jesus cannot be bought.
It is simply a tangible way to support the continued creation and distribution of Christ-centered teaching, discipleship resources, and Gospel content so more people can encounter biblical truth.
Matthew left his booth because Jesus was worth following.
The Gospel still confronts every generation with the same Christ.
You can accumulate money and still be poor toward God.
You can lose the world's applause and discover eternal treasure.
You can carry a scandalous past and still encounter astonishing grace.
Because when Jesus becomes the center of the story, your worst chapter does not have to write your ending.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because the greatest thing Matthew ever received was not whatever income passed through his hands.
It was the moment Christ passed by his booth...
and Matthew finally discovered something worth getting up for.
